nodes.question: What were the third and fourth most important priorities mentioned in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The third and fourth most important priorities were economic prosperity and economic growth, respectively.
nodes.paragraph: Economic prosperity and economic growth were also highly valued, as the third and fourth most important priorities, respectively. There are identifiable differences in how younger and older Australians prioritise a restored natural world, a life lived with dignity and economic prosperity. R. Milte et al. 1 Introduction In 2018, prior to the onset of the global COVID-19 pan - demic, governments from six developed countries (Scot - land, New Zealand, Iceland, Wales, Finland and Canada) combined to form the Wellbeing Economy Alliance (WEAII), an international network promoting a new way of economic thinking [1 ]. The WEAII rejects traditional economic indicators such as the maximisation of economic growth at any cost and instead aims to advance the key principles of a wellbeing economy; ensuring an equita- ble distribution of wealth and wellbeing, where caring is highly valued and where the planet S resources are pro- tected [1 4]. The advent of the global coronavirus dis- ease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic has further exposed the cracks in the economic fabric of societies. In addition, it has provided a unique opportunity for reflection and the potential for a collective reset to advance the principles of a wellbeing economy in a post-pandemic world [3 ].

nodes.question: What was the main objective of the study discussed in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The main objective of the study was to assess the relative importance of the key principles of a wellbeing economy to the Australian general public and to investigate the preferences across different demographic subgroups.
nodes.paragraph: Similarly to those proposed by WEAII and Measuring What Matters, these indicators are cross-sectoral in that they include indicators commonly reported on by dif- ferent government departments (for example, health, treas- ury, education, labour and environment). While these indi- cators can all be considered important within an individual department and fall within their remit, some of our most intractable societal problems are cross-sectional in nature. These problems are likely to require cooperation across mul- tiple stakeholders to solve. Whilst the principles of a wellbe- ing economy are increasingly being embraced by policymak - ers, to our knowledge no study to date has sought to identify the preferences of the general public for the principles of a wellbeing economy as countries re-build following the dis- ruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. This study aimed to fill this gap in our current knowledge by assessing the relative importance to the Australian gen- eral public of the key principles of a wellbeing economy and to investigate the potential for heterogeneity in preferences in relation to these key principles between demographic subgroups. 2 Methods 2.1 Survey An online survey was developed and delivered to a sample of Australian adults (aged 18 years and above).
